title: SIU charge Toronto Police officer with criminal negligence causing death
subtitle: The SIU have charged a Toronto Police officer following an investigation into how he allegedly handled a situation involving a suicidal man in High Park.
article: The province's police watchdog has charged a Toronto cop over his unspecified involvement with a suicidal man in High Park last winter.

In a news release Thursday, the Special Investigations Unit announced that, after a recently completed inquiry, Toronto police Const. Kyle Upjohn has been charged with criminal negligence causing death, and failing to provide the necessities of life.

The SIU statement said police were contacted around 2 p.m. on Feb. 2, regarding a suicide attempt by a 19-year-old man inside the west-end park. By 3:30 p.m., the SIU wrote, the 19-year-old was pronounced dead.
No other details were provided. The deceased man's name has never been released and is unknown to the Star.

The SIU investigates instances across Ontario where a civilian is seriously injured, killed, or sexually assaulted during an interaction with police. In an email, Jason Gennaro, spokesperson for the agency, declined to elaborate on this investigation's findings because the matter is before the courts.

Later Thursday afternoon, Toronto police Chief Mark Saunders told reporters he can't talk about Upjohn's charges. "When the SIU invokes a mandate, we're not allowed to talk, so by law I can't talk," he said.
Toronto Police Association president Mike McCormack, meanwhile, was not available to comment on Thursday, according to his assistant.
A man who answered the front door at Upjohn's home on Thursday said, "Nothing to say. Goodbye," and shut the door. Upjohn is schedule to appear in court at Old City Hall on Aug. 4.

The charges come amidst calls for the reform of police oversight and accountability. There were protests earlier this year after the SIU decided not to charge the Toronto police officer who shot and killed 45-year-old Andrew Loku last summer. In the face of public pressure and calls for transparency, Ontario's Attorney General released nine of 34 pages from the SIU investigation report into Loku's death.
It was the first time since the creation of the SIU in 1990 that part of a report was made public.

In May, Attorney General Madeleine Meilleur announced that all SIU reports could be released retroactively as part of the province's police oversight review. That could include thousands of secret documents related to its investigations, as well as details of more than 130 fatal police shootings the agency has probed.
Court of Appeal Justice Michael Tulloch has been tapped by the province to head the police oversight review.
The government says Tulloch's final recommendations will be submitted to the Attorney General by March 2017.

In a separate incident, the SIU started another investigation this week - this time in relation to a 19-year-old man who was treated for "serious facial injuries " after he was arrested by Toronto police on Tuesday.
The watchdog said in a news release that an undercover officer was involved in "an interaction" with two men outside a house in Etobicoke, before other officers were called in to help.
